text:
No, I am smiling. This is to be my way of smiling. I
want this grimace to be my own.

She listens to these short, hoarse words and does not understand them,
does not comprehend them at all. What can he mean?

But suddenly he throws his arms around her, iron-hard,
with terrifying strength, and whispers close to her face:

What do you say to our putting horns on him .... on him who
left .... to our putting horns on him?
She utters a scream and calls the maid. He releases her
with a quiet, dry laugh, opening his mouth wide like
a maw and slapping both his thighs.

In the morning the lady’s good heart again prevails, and
she says to her husband:

You had a peculiar fit last night; it is over now, of course;
but you are pale today as well.

Yes, he replies, it is taxing to be witty at my
age. I shall never be so again.

But after speaking of many kinds of love, the
monk Vendt tells of yet another kind and says:

For so intoxicating is a particular kind of love!

The young master and mistress have just come home, their long wedding
journey is at an end, and they retire for the night.

A shooting star burned out above their roof.

In summer the young master and mistress walked together and did
not leave each other’s side. They picked yellow, red, and blue flowers
which they gave to each other; they watched the grass move in the wind and
heard the birds singing in the forests, and every word they spoke was like
a caress. In winter they drove with bells on the horses, and
the sky was blue, and high above, the stars rushed away across the
eternal plains.

Thus many, many years passed. The young master and mistress had three children,
and their hearts loved each other as on the first day beneath the
first kiss.

Then the proud gentleman was stricken with his illness, the illness that
chained him to his bed for so long and put his wife’s patience
to so hard a test. On the day he recovered and rose from the bed,
he did not recognize himself; the illness had disfigured
him and taken his hair.

He suffered and brooded. Then one morning he said:

Now you no longer love me, do you?

But his wife, blushing, threw her arms around him and kissed
him as passionately as in the springtime of youth, and answered:

I, I love, love you always. I never forget that it
was I and no other whom you took, and who became so
happy.

And she went into her chamber and cut all the yellow hair from
her head so as to resemble her husband, whom she loved.

And again many, many years passed; the young master and mistress grew
old, and their children were grown. They shared every happiness as
before; in summer they still walked in the fields and watched the grass
wave, and in winter they wrapped themselves in their furs and drove beneath
the starry sky. And their hearts continued to be warm and
glad, as though from wondrous wine.

Then the lady became paralyzed. The old lady could not walk on her
feet; she had to be pulled in a wheeled chair, and the gentleman himself
pulled her. But the lady suffered so unspeakably from her misfortune, and her
face acquired deep furrows of sorrow.

Then one day she said:

Now I should like to die. I am so paralyzed and ugly, and your face
is so beautiful; you cannot kiss me anymore, and you cannot love
me as before.

But the gentleman embraces her, red with emotion, and answers:

I, I love you more, more than my life, my dear one; I love
you as on the first day, the first moment when you gave me the rose.
Do you remember it? You held out the rose to me and looked at me with your
beautiful eyes; the rose was fragrant like you, you blushed like it, and I
became intoxicated in all my senses. But I love you even more
now; you are more beautiful than in your youth, and my heart thanks and
blesses you for every day you have been mine.

The gentleman goes into his chamber, dashes acid into his face to
disfigure it, and says to his wife:

I had the misfortune to get acid in my face; my cheeks are
covered with burns, and you no longer love me, do you?

Oh, you my bridegroom, my beloved! stammers the old woman
and kisses his hands. You are more beautiful than any man on
earth; your voice makes my heart hot even to this very day,
and I love you unto death.

XIII

Johannes meets Camilla in the street; she is with her
mother, her father, and young Richmond; they stop their carriage and speak
kindly to him.

Camilla takes his arm and says:

You did not come to see us. We had a grand celebration, you may be sure;
we waited for you until the very end, but you did not come.

I was prevented, he replied.

Forgive me for not having been up to see you since, she continued.
I shall come one of these days, quite certainly, when Richmond
has left. Oh, what a celebration we had! Victoria became ill; she was
driven home, have you heard? I shall be going up to see her soon.
She is surely much better, perhaps entirely well again. I have
given Richmond a medallion almost identical to yours. Listen, Johannes,
you must promise me to tend your stove; when you write, you forget
everything, and it becomes icy cold at your place. Then you must ring for
the maid.
Yes, I shall ring for the maid, he replied.

Mrs. Seier also spoke to him, asked about his work, about
the play about The Family; how was it going? She awaited his next
one with longing.

Johannes gave the necessary answers, bowed very deeply, and watched
the carriage drive away. How little the whole thing concerned him—this carriage,
these people, this chatter! An empty and cold mood entered
him and followed him all the way home. At his gate
a man was loitering back and forth in the street, an old
acquaintance, the former tutor at the Castle.

Johannes greeted him.

He was dressed in a long, warm coat that had been carefully
brushed, and he wore a bold and resolute expression.

Here You see Your friend and colleague, he said. Give me Your
hand, young man. God has guided my paths wondrously since
last time; I am married, I have a home, a little garden, a wife. Miracles
still happen in life. Have You anything to remark upon my last statement?

Johannes looks at him in astonishment.

Then it is settled. You see, I tutored her son. She has
a son; the brat is from her first marriage; she had naturally been
married before, she was a widow. Thus I married a widow. You
may object that this was not sung at my cradle; but I
did, then, marry a widow. She had the brat already. I walk
about there, you see, looking at the garden and the widow, and live for a while
with intense thoughts on that subject. Suddenly I have it,
and I say to myself: very well, it was not sung at your
cradle, and so forth; but I do it all the same, I take the plunge, for
it is presumably written in the stars. There, that is how it happened.
